u1-emuA:
Note that trying a different rule doesn't necessarily require everyone to go buy land. It could be first tried internally to the group, then as semi-autonomous groups within the same group, then as seed groups that still share some resources (tools, child care, business or friendship links) and are physically close, and then as a complete split could be just one step along a gradient of seperation.

Morevoer, the experiments of trying different land rules, or population sizes, or any number of different rules may not be able to be done cheaply, and may not look good without the assets to make them work.

One more problem that will have to be solved, if we want these communities to spread, is how to deal with each other without forming a super-commune, which is essentially the state. We want some way of connecting up, helping each other, sharing people and knowledge, but without being all the same.

Out there, we need to spread and help heal the world. We need to train and spread out, and we need to not be complacent in our enclaves.

The Federation of Egalitarian Communties is trying to get it together again, but keep in mind that it takes work to run a federation: delegates, records, making sure people are doing what they are supposed to, marshalling resources, meetings, succession and dispute function, and so on, not to mention a reserve of money from outside the communities if you have to deal with the law or economy at that level. It also doesn't need to all be done at one level; two communities can be friend communities and also be in a general federation with other communities, there can be local federations of close communities, there can be single-function federations (like the health pooling organization that the FEC helped to form, PEACH, which is not currently governed by the FEC delegates), and so on.

One key to this whole thing is to cooperate without merging. The FEC has full members, groups working toward full membership, and groups that may just want to be Friends and not do the whole thing. Also, people need to be able to move between communities, and it takes work to set up the housing, status, health, records, labor, travel, tax, dispute and other transitional issues so that people can move between groups without starting from scratch each time. Fortunately, that interface can be thin, and groups don't have to have the same internal systems for this to work.

Finally, even if we don't use money internally, we have to have some way of keeping track of what's going on between the groups, whether it's food, medicine, vehicles, tools, labor, emergency housing, construction help, or visits for training or building. Different types of exchanges need to be tracked for different purposes, but it doesn't need to all be "even". The fed can keep track of all these different types of exchanges. If we use cash for dealing with the outside world, it will also need to keep track of grants and loans in and out of the federation. Also, while we're all solidary with each other, we need to keep track of guarantees and enterprise commitments separately; we're not going to be able to hold each other liable for all the debts of the other groups, nor can we draw on each other's labor, stores, land and tools indefinitely.

When you create a rule to deal with a collision of two principles, you should store the hard case that the rule is meant to deal with, the principles involved, your first judgments, your final decision and rationale, any dissenting opinions, and what happens when you apply the rule, and which version of the rule you applied it under. When the rule changes, run the case through again. This saves you from having to redo all the constitutional cases each generation.
u1-emuB:
Related to, but not the same as, is a way of allowing people to try another way of doing things, without requiring them to go buy their own land. Trying it out in the context of the parent group, maybe as a semi-autonomous unit, maybe as a group that is preparing to become a seed group nearby, sharing some functions like tool library or childcare or some business or just by friendship, is a step. It should be a gradient of options, with breaking off completely being one of them.

Some things will require, in order to be tried at all, that you have different amounts of land, different population, a whole bundle of different rules, and so on, and you can't try it cheaply. Trying them in a context that lacks those assets would make them look worse than they might be.

And then when we want to spread out, we need some solution to the problem of how to not be a giant super-commune (which is just the state over again). Connecting up with other communities of similar sort, helping each other, moving people and knowledge around, but not losing our distinctness, is something that I do want.

At the level of federation, we want to be spreading out our ways of doing things (like healing), training people, seeding, making sure that the people who are settling into nice enclaces don't forget about the idea of spreading it.

One organization that does try to do this, The Federation of Egalitarian Communities , seems to me to be rebuilding itself now. But it will take work to do this - there will be people doing the federation work, being delegates, recording, making sure that people are doing what the federation said they would do, or whatever is the federation's job, making the federation able to coordinate resources, and so on. Taking the time to meet, set up successors, and deal with the job of the federation when there is a dispute to arbitrate, and all the rest of the things that federations do. It will need material resources to do this, possibly even outside money if our legal and economic context requires it. This may or may not be done by one entity, it may be that two communities that are close friends want to coordinate things and share resources in a tighter configuration than is appropriate for the general federation, and it may be that there are local clusters that want to do this or other institutions that do one function (like the PEC health pool PEACH that is not yet governed by the FEC delegates).

One thing to notice about coordinating is that it doesn't necessarily mean merging, and that there are different levels of participating for different purposes. The FEC has full members, people who are working towards becoming full members, and "Friends" who may never do more than be friends. Also related to this, we need to let people move from one to another. And not just in theory, but in practice, in terms of housing and status and health and record keeping and labor and transportation and taxes and dealing with problems that come up at transition time. Presumably a thin interface will be able to do this, and not require that the different systems the communities have internally be all the same.

Related to this, even if we don't use money, it may be useful to have some way of keeping track of how much of each thing we exchange with each other, what we owe to each other, how much food we share, how much medicine, transportation in vehicles or tools, trades of labor, emergency housing, building projects, visits for training or for relationship building, and so on. We may want to keep track of these things separately for different purposes, but they don't need to be all "even" or use money to keep track of them. If we use cash to transact with the outside world, we may want to keep track of grants and loans of cash. But if we are not legally separate, just because we say we have solidarity, it doesn't mean that we are all responsible for each other's debts, and it doesn't mean that all our labor, or stores, or land, or tools, are all equally available to all the communities. It may be that we commit to working some enterprise together, but that is also something to keep track of separately.

When a conflict between two principles leads to the formulation of a rule, keep the original case on file, what happened, what principles were involved, what judgments were made, what was finally decided, what the rationale was, what the dissenting opinions were, what the consequences were, and under what version of the rule it was decided. When the rule changes, re-run the case. This will prevent a lot of re-running of "constitutional issues".
